claims.text: Correctness (R5, R6, R13): the case pipeline applies the profile. A director's or shareholder's name makes a credit director_funding even with an invoice reference; an own account's name makes lines own_account_transfer in both directions, out of M2 and M9; the proposed repayment feeds M28 (n/a with the reason without one); the workspace summary shows each profile field. Tested through /api/case on a real server, on cases with and without each field.

Escalation major (v1 precedence, credits): under v1 a protected verdict by the term decides before a profile name. JANE DOE LOAN is v1:loan_drawdown, REFUND JANE DOE stays v1's own rule, and director wording decides before two profile kinds make a credit ambiguous. The v2 case gives the same verdicts.

claims.text: Docs: README's categoriser row now says that a profile name never settles an ambiguous credit and only adds a candidate. It also states the both-kinds rule under v1 and v2, and lists the v1 rules that give a protected verdict. It previously said that the profile naming the payer settles such a credit.

Observability and operability: the tool is local-only and has no remote alerting, by design (design Observability). Each line records its rule id (profile:director, profile:own_account, v1:<rule>, <ruleset>:conflict:...), which proves which verdict ran. Rollback is CMA_RULESET or a reinstall. A profile applies under v1 by R54.

notes: Gaps for the owner (design, not code): (1) The v1 protected set (_V1_PROTECTED and _V1_PROTECTED_IN in categorise.py) is a list in code beside the pinned v1 table, chosen by reading the term 'protected verdict' against v1's rules. v1's non_trading_in rule mixes protected wording (DIRECTOR, REFUND, HMRC...) with bare words (CAPITAL, SAVINGS, INTEREST, GRANT), and only the former counts. The owner should confirm the list, for example whether bare CAPITAL or SAVINGS under v1 should outrank a profile name. Under v1, IWOCA wording is no lender, so the name decides IWOCA JANE DOE ACME HOLDINGS there, as v1 lists no lenders. (2) No remote alert exists by design.
